claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-built microstructure contains microscale elemental heterogeneities.
The as-built alloy contains residual porosity.
The as-built alloy has grain-boundary compositional variability.
At elevated temperature, grain boundaries act as fast diffusion paths that enhance oxygen ingress.
Elevated-temperature gas exposure can cause localized depletion or redistribution of Cr and Al at grain boundaries.
Preferential grain-boundary reactions form oxide or secondary phases.
The grain-boundary oxide or secondary phases are brittle and weaken intergranular cohesion.
Under reducing conditions, redistribution of key elements destabilizes grain-boundary chemistry even when oxidation is limited.
Exposure-induced grain-boundary alteration reduces ductility.
Exposure-induced grain-boundary alteration reduces fracture toughness.
Loss of grain-boundary cohesion can trigger catastrophic failure under mechanical stress.
Moderately oxidizing exposure will produce thicker grain-boundary oxide layers than an inert-atmosphere baseline.
Moderately oxidizing exposure will decrease fracture toughness relative to the inert-atmosphere baseline.
Moderately oxidizing exposure will decrease ductility relative to the inert-atmosphere baseline.
Degradation under reducing conditions will be less pronounced than under oxidizing conditions but may remain measurable if elemental redistribution occurs.
The likelihood or severity of catastrophic failure will correlate with the degree of grain-boundary modification.
The as-fabricated inert baseline has homogeneous grain boundaries.
The proposed degradation effects become significant at approximately 600 °C or above.
The proposed degradation becomes more pronounced as oxygen partial pressure increases.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as having grain-boundary compositional variability, whereas the nominally same as-fabricated baseline is described as retaining homogeneous grain boundaries.
